corpus_definition: A connection between two things or places.

forms.definition: a connection between two things, people or places
forms.example: There is a strong link between diet and health.
forms.note: On a website, a link is the word or picture you click to go to another page.

syn.note: Almost the same meaning and very common.
Used for links between people, families or countries: 'close ties'.
Related: the way two things or people are connected.
Related: a strong feeling that connects people.

forms.definition: the way two or more things are joined or connected
forms.example: Scientists are studying the linkage between the two problems.

forms.definition: to join or connect two things or places
forms.example: A new bridge links the two villages.

syn.note: Same meaning, very common.
Join often means putting things together so they become one.
Related: to show that two ideas are connected.
Related: to connect two things in your mind.

ant.note: To keep things apart instead of joining them.
To break a connection, for example a cable or the internet.

forms.definition: connected with each other in some way
forms.example: Stress and poor sleep are closely linked.

syn.note: Same meaning, very common.
Often used for ideas, problems or people in a family.

ant.note: Having no connection at all.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: The new road links our village to Tashkent. Before, there was no good link between the two places. Now the two towns are closely linked by road and rail.

reviewer_note: Corpus example uses the website sense; map keeps the general 'connection' meaning and mentions the website use in a note. Hyperlink is a compound and is left out.

corpus_definition: Full of energy and very active.

forms.definition: the quality of being full of energy and fun
forms.example: I love the liveliness of the bazaar in the morning.

syn.note: Easy word; energy is the power to be active.
More formal; often about a person's health and energy.
Related: a happy, brave or active attitude.

ant.note: The quality of being boring and without energy.

forms.definition: to make something more exciting or full of energy
forms.example: Some music will liven up the party.
forms.note: Almost always used as 'liven up': 'liven up a room', 'the party livened up'.

syn.note: Related: to make a place or a person's mood happier.
Related: to make someone feel happier; easy phrasal verb.
To give energy to people or a place. British spelling: energise.

forms.definition: full of energy, noise and activity
forms.example: It was a very lively party last night.

syn.note: Very close; energetic is often about people.
Often about cities, colors and places full of life.
Easy word; doing a lot of things.
Related: a busy place has many people, but it is not always fun.
Related: happy and positive.

ant.note: Boring, with nothing interesting happening.
With little noise or activity.

forms.note: There is no common adverb; say 'in a lively way'.

context.text: The Chorsu market in Tashkent is always lively in the morning. At my cousin's wedding a band played to liven up the evening, and everyone enjoyed the liveliness of the music.

reviewer_note: Lively is an adjective even though it ends in -ly; no adverb form is shown.

corpus_definition: Money that is borrowed and must be given back later.

forms.definition: money that a bank or person lends you and you must pay back
forms.example: He took out a bank loan for his car.

syn.note: Related: an arrangement to buy now and pay later.
Related: the money you still have to pay back.
A special kind of bank money for buying a house or flat.

forms.definition: to lend something to someone, especially money
forms.example: My uncle loaned me the money for my studies.
forms.note: More common in American English; in British English people usually say 'lend'.

syn.note: Same meaning and the more common word, especially in British English.
Related: to give someone money before the usual time.

ant.note: The person who gets the money borrows it; the other person loans it.

forms.note: There is no adjective; we use the phrase 'on loan'.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Akmal took out a loan from the bank to buy a car. His brother also loaned him some money, so now he has to pay back two loans.

reviewer_note: Lender and borrower name the people but come from lend and borrow, not from loan.

particle_note: Usually used without an object: 'log off'. With the system: 'log off the computer' or 'log off from the website'. Past: logged off.

relations.note: Same meaning; log out is more common today.
Same meaning, common on websites and apps.
Related: to close a program or leave a place.
To start using a computer system with your name and password.
To enter a system with your name and password.

context.text: Remember to log off before you leave the office. Yesterday Sardor forgot, and his colleague logged off for him.

reviewer_note: Phrasal verb; antonyms log on / log in kept in relations.

corpus_definition: To start using a computer program by entering your name.
particle_note: Not separable. Used alone ('I can't log on') or with to: 'log on to the website' (also written 'log onto'). Past: logged on.

relations.note: Same meaning; log in is more common today.
Same meaning, common on websites and apps.
Related: to go into a place or type information.
To stop using a computer system.
To leave a system so others cannot use your account.

context.text: You need a password to log on. Every morning Madina logs on to the school website to check her homework.

reviewer_note: Phrasal verb; 'log on to' vs 'log onto' spelling noted.

corpus_definition: A round shape created by a line crossing itself.

forms.definition: a round shape made when a line, rope or string crosses itself
forms.example: Tie the rope into a small loop.

syn.note: Related: a closed circle, but a ring does not cross itself.
Related: an easy word for any round shape.
Related: many loops of rope or wire, one on top of another.

forms.definition: to make something into a round shape, or move in a circle
forms.example: He looped the rope around the tree.

syn.note: To turn something around another thing many times.
To make many loops, one on top of another.
Related: to turn something around itself.
Related: to make a small curved shape.

ant.note: To make something straight again.

forms.definition: a little crazy or strange
forms.example: My little brother gets a bit loopy when he is tired.
forms.note: Informal. Belongs to a different meaning (crazy, silly), not the round shape.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Dilnoza tied the ribbon into a loop on top of the gift box. Then she looped a second ribbon around it to make it look nicer.

reviewer_note: Loopy (informal 'crazy') shown as other_meaning; loophole is a compound and is left out.

corpus_definition: Showing that you care a lot about someone.

forms.definition: a very strong, warm feeling of caring about someone
forms.example: A mother's love for her children is very strong.

syn.note: A gentle, warm feeling of liking someone.
Weaker: liking someone or something a lot.
Related: looking after someone because they matter to you.

ant.note: A very strong feeling of not liking someone.
A strong, lasting feeling of hate.

forms.definition: to have very strong, warm feelings for someone
forms.example: I love my grandparents very much.

syn.note: Stronger: to love someone very much.
Softer; also means to look after someone.
Related but much weaker.

ant.note: To have a very strong feeling of not liking someone.

forms.definition: showing that you care a lot about someone
forms.example: She comes from a very loving family.

syn.note: Very close and easy.
Showing love, often with hugs and kind words.
Friendly and kind.
Loving someone and giving them a lot of time and help.
Related: nice to other people, but not always with love.

ant.note: Not showing any warm feelings.
Not showing love; rare and formal.

forms.definition: easy to like and care about
forms.example: Their new puppy is very lovable.

forms.definition: very beautiful, nice or pleasant
forms.example: We had a lovely day in the mountains.
forms.note: Belongs to love = like something very much (nice, pleasant), not caring about someone.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you care a lot
forms.example: Grandma lovingly made plov for the whole family.

syn.note: In a gentle, caring way.
In a way that shows love.
Often used for memories: 'remember fondly'.
Related: in a friendly way.

ant.note: In an unfriendly way, without warm feelings.

people.definition: a person who enjoys something very much
people.example: My father is a big football lover.
people.note: Belongs to love = enjoy something (music lover, animal lover). Alone, 'lover' often means a romantic partner.

context.text: Nodira grew up in a loving family in Bukhara. Her grandmother always spoke lovingly about the old days, and the children felt her love every day.

reviewer_note: Headword is the -ing adjective; love (noun/verb) is its root. Lovely is a false friend (nice), shown as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Always staying on the side of your friends.

forms.definition: the quality of always supporting a person, group or country
forms.example: The team's fans show great loyalty every season.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little less common.
Strong love and support for someone.
Formal; usually to a country, leader or group.

ant.note: Not supporting your friends, country or group.
Hurting someone who trusted you.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: always supporting your friends and never leaving them
forms.example: Dogs are known for being very loyal.

syn.note: Very close; also used for husbands and wives.
Giving someone a lot of love and time.
Easy word: 'a true friend'.
Related: you can trust them to do what they promise.

ant.note: Not supporting your friends or group.
Not faithful, often to a husband or wife.

forms.definition: in a way that always supports someone
forms.example: He has loyally supported the same football team for twenty years.

syn.note: Same meaning.
With a lot of love and support.

people.definition: a person who keeps supporting a leader or government, especially in hard times
people.example: The king's loyalists stayed with him until the end.

context.text: My dog Bobik is very loyal; he waits for me at the gate every evening. His loyalty makes the whole family happy.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (B1). Disloyal/disloyalty are opposites, so they sit in ant lists.

corpus_definition: Two organs in the chest used for taking in air.

forms.definition: the two organs in your chest that you breathe with
forms.example: Smoking is very bad for your lungs.

syn.note: Related: the part of the body where these organs are.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
Doctors use 'pulmonary', but it comes from Latin, not from this word.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: The fresh mountain air in Chimgan is good for your lungs. My doctor says I should stop smoking to keep my lungs healthy.

reviewer_note: Headword is plural in the corpus; singular lung mentioned in the note. Only one form exists, so context uses one form.

corpus_definition: something very expensive and comfortable, not a basic need

forms.definition: something expensive and pleasant that you do not really need
forms.example: Staying in that hotel was a real luxury for them.
forms.note: Also used before nouns: a luxury hotel, a luxury car.

syn.note: Spending a lot of money on something you do not need.
Related: something special and nice that you do not have often.
Related: a pleasant, easy feeling; not always expensive.
Related: something you allow yourself for pleasure.

ant.note: Something you really need, like food or a home.

forms.definition: to relax and enjoy something very pleasant and comfortable
forms.example: After the long walk, she luxuriated in a hot bath.

syn.note: To enjoy something warm or pleasant, like the sun.
Related: an easy word for resting and feeling calm.

forms.definition: very comfortable, beautiful and expensive
forms.example: They stayed in a luxurious hotel in Samarkand.

syn.note: Very rich and expensive, often more than needed.
Informal; expensive and elegant.
Related: costing a lot of money.
Related: pleasant to sit in or live in.

ant.note: Plain and without expensive extras.
With only the things you really need.

forms.definition: growing thickly and well, like plants or hair
forms.example: She has long, luxuriant hair.
forms.note: False friend: luxuriant means growing thick and strong, not expensive. Don't confuse with luxurious.

forms.definition: in a very comfortable and expensive way
forms.example: The rooms are luxuriously decorated with silk and gold.

syn.note: In a rich and expensive way.
Related: in a pleasant, easy way.

ant.note: In a plain way, without expensive extras.

context.text: For our anniversary we stayed in a luxurious hotel in Tashkent. It was a real luxury for us, and the rooms were luxuriously decorated.

reviewer_note: False-friend trap: luxuriant (growing thickly) vs luxurious; luxuriant shown as other_meaning.
